## Simple explanation

Negative log-likelihood (NLL) penalizes a model when it gives low
probability to the correct answer. A model that assigns high probability
to what actually happened receives a smaller loss.

## Technical explanation

For observed outcomes $y_1,\ldots,y_n$ and model parameters $\theta$, the
likelihood is $L(\theta)=\prod_i p_\theta(y_i)$. Its negative log is:

$$
\operatorname{NLL}(\theta)
= -\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log p_\theta(y_i)
$$

The average NLL divides this sum by the number of examples. Minimizing NLL
is equivalent to maximizing the likelihood when the data are fixed.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

NLL is a standard objective for probabilistic prediction, including
classification and language modeling. It rewards assigning probability to
the observed target and strongly penalizes confidently wrong predictions.
It is also useful for comparing probabilistic forecasts when computed on
the same evaluation data and convention.

## How it works

For each example, the model produces a probability distribution and the
loss selects the probability assigned to the observed target, takes its
logarithm, and negates it. In classification with one-hot labels this is
the cross-entropy loss. Numerical implementations generally operate on
logits directly for stability.

## Practical example

If a classifier assigns probability $0.9$ to the correct class, its
per-example NLL is $-\log(0.9)$. If it assigns only $0.01$, the loss is
much larger, reflecting a poor and confident prediction.

## Common misconceptions

- NLL is small when probability on the observed outcome is high; it is not itself a probability.
- Summed NLL and mean NLL have different scales, so confirm the reduction used when comparing values.
- A lower training NLL does not guarantee better performance on unseen data.
